title: Please qualify your various comments on paragraphs
body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

I have concerns that the specification is doing the opposite of creating clarity in its guidance regarding [paragraphs](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#paragraphs).

> A paragraph is typically a run of [phrasing content](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#phrasing-content-2) that forms a block of text with one or more sentences that discuss a particular topic, as in typography, but can also be used for more general thematic grouping. For instance, an address is also a paragraph, as is a part of a form, a byline, or a stanza in a poem.

These grouping examples are problematic. An address is not linguistically a paragraph. There is a semantic element for address, so why state an address should use a paragraph element?

Since a `form` is a section, "part of a form" _could_ contain a paragraph of instructional text. But it is much more likely to contain labels, inputs and other elements which are not paragraphs. The example is insufficient to provide any clarity. Similarly, "byline" is an undefined term without any useful context.

That leaves poetry. A stanza of in a poem _may_ be a paragraph. Robert Frost's [Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/42891/stopping-by-woods-on-a-snowy-evening) is a good example of something that most accurately can be described as a construct of four paragraphs with line breaks.

A stanza of poetry can also very clearly not be a lingustic paragraph. William Carlos Williams' [The Red Wheelbarrow](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45502/the-red-wheelbarrow) springs to mind. This can  most accurately be described as four divs with line breaks.

In both these cases, I am using the content to inform decisions on the most appropriate code to reflect the linguistic reality.

Overall, the inference in the spec is that any grouping of text is a paragraph, and any element that can be used to group chunks of text is therefore valid.

This guidance is causing knock-on effects in interpretation and clarity with WCAG requirements. The latest example is https://github.com/w3c/wcag/issues/4759. I would ask some of what I believe is non-normative guidance to more clearly distinguish between what is technically possible and what is most appropriate.
